subject: dragonfly
pitch: An emperor dragonfly hovering above a pond. A long, slim abdomen in electric blue with black markings down its back, an apple-green thorax, huge wraparound turquoise eyes, and four glassy wings with a fine net of dark veins and a faint golden sheen, held flat and wide. Six thin legs are tucked under it.
reasoning:
I'm planning a single TypeScript module built with the SDK, keeping the hovering model's lowest point above the ground at a fixed height, and sizing it realistically based on an emperor dragonfly's body length and wingspan.

I'm working out the coordinate layout now: head and thorax forward, abdomen extending back roughly 10 cm, wings spanning about 5.5 cm to each side, with the whole body hovering at a set height with legs tucked rather than resting on a pond surface prop.

Now I'm starting to assemble the skeleton with the SDK, defining the thorax as the root joint, the head joint aimed forward, and an abdomen chain built from a sequence of catmull-spline points curving downward and back.

I'm thinking through the abdomen's radius profile — slim and roughly uniform like a dragonfly's, narrowing slightly toward the tip with a subtle sine-based taper, before moving on to coloring.

For colors I'm picking electric blue, black, apple green, and turquoise eyes, with pale translucent-looking wings. Since the material doesn't support real transparency or textures, I'm considering painting fine vein lines onto the wing geometry procedurally using a coordinate-based pattern rather than an actual texture map.

I'm working out wing orientation and geometry: figuring out which axes define the outline plane versus thickness so the wings lie flat and spread horizontally, computing the extrusion vectors needed for that orientation.

Now I'm sketching the forewing's actual outline coordinates, placing the root near the thorax and tracing out a narrow-to-wide rounded shape with leading and trailing edges.

For the hindwing I'm offsetting the same silhouette slightly backward and making it marginally larger, then setting a thin tapering thickness so the wings read as flat, near-horizontal membranes at hover position. For coloring I'm planning a translucent, glassy wing tint with a faint golden sheen using a noise-based paint mix rather than a flat color.

I'm sketching out a vein pattern for the wings using a grid-based threshold function in surface coordinates, but the resulting line width comes out far too thin to be visible, so I'll need to widen the grid spacing or threshold tolerance.

For positioning the wing pair, I'm using mirrored x-axis extrusion so both wings share the same outline but flip orientation across the body midline, with the root anchored near the centerline and the outline extruding outward from there.

Now I'm thinking through the legs: six thin tucked legs in three pairs (front, middle, hind), each built as a chain of hip-knee-ankle joints, with the front pair curving forward under the head and the others spaced along the thorax and abdomen base.

Working out leg joint positions for front and middle legs, tucking them under the thorax with hip-knee-tip paths angled outward and down for a folded resting posture.

I'm defining the abdomen as a chain off the thorax root, curving downward and back using a catmull spline through a few control points, then planning dorsal black stripe sectors to overlay on the blue body coloring.

For the coloring, I'm using a paint function based on the segment angle and position along the chain to create alternating dorsal bands, keeping everything blue with black stripes. For the sweep radius, I'm settling on a profile that stays thin near the thorax and widens slightly toward the tip, giving the abdomen a gentle taper with a slightly clubbed end, using round caps.

Now for the thorax, I'm building it as a scaled sphere geometry attached to the thorax bone, giving it an elongated ellipsoid shape colored green, and adding black shoulder stripes either as small separate box parts or via a paint function that uses the normal vector to detect side regions for the stripe pattern.

For the head, I'm planning a small dark sphere for the base plus two large turquoise sphere eyes positioned symmetrically on either side, sized and offset to mimic the oversized dragonfly eye look dominating the small head.

I'm also sketching a facet pattern using a cellular (Worley) noise function on the eye surface, coloring the thin ridges between cells dark and the cell interiors turquoise to fake the ommatidia texture. Then I'm setting up the head joint attached to the thorax with its own position and orientation before building the head and eye geometry parts.

Now I'm positioning small antenna rods extending up from the head, then moving on to wing attachment points on the thorax, planning separate root positions and local axis orientations for the forewing and hindwing so their outline shapes extrude in the right directions.

For the outline shapes, I'm sketching point arrays for the forewing and hindwing contours, but I decide to drop the "sharp" corner markers since they could cause a type mismatch and instead rely on smoothing with extra points to approximate the wing silhouettes. I settle on keeping the wings flat and level, mirrored left and right with a thin extrusion thickness, attached to the thorax bone.

Now I'm designing the wing paint function: creating a vein grid by checking horizontal, vertical, and diagonal grid-cell proximity, with a noise-based sheen determining whether a cell renders pale yellow or pale blue, and fixing negative modulo issues with a fractional-part helper so the grid doesn't break for negative coordinates. I tune the vein spacing to roughly 5mm for a net-like pattern and confirm the noise call operates correctly in model space.

Then I move to the abdomen paint, deciding dorsal segments show black bands against electric blue sides using the surface normal's y-component to distinguish top from sides, combined with a repeating fractional pattern along the body length to create segment stripes. For the thorax I set up black stripes on the sides against a green base using the normal's x-component and a z-based repeating pattern. For the legs, I plan a thin black sweep along a polyline chain with round caps to keep them dark and spiny like an emperor dragonfly's legs.

Now I'm working out the skeleton structure: leg chains parented to the thorax with three named joints (hip, knee, tip) using the "leg" role, an abdomen chain built from a catmull curve parented to the thorax with a "tail" role and three abdomen joints, and a head joint positioned slightly forward and up from the thorax for the eyes to attach to. I'm also considering the hover pose, keeping the body mostly horizontal but letting the abdomen tilt up slightly as real dragonflies do when hovering.

Now I'm defining leg positions for both sides, setting up front, middle, and hind leg joint coordinates.

Skipping extra spine details and finalizing the abdomen proportions at roughly 5.6mm diameter, matching an emperor dragonfly's build. Now moving to defining the thorax paint/coloring.

Now I'm defining the wing paint function, which draws a vein grid pattern using fractional spacing along both local axes plus a diagonal grid, then fills the remaining cells with a gold-or-clear noise pattern.

I'm picking subtler colors for the veins, gold sheen, and clear areas so the gold doesn't overpower the glass look, and refining toward softer tones before finalizing.
